Article Title: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei once wrote that saying AI will cure cancer is 'more a cliché than it is inspiring'; now, he tells IPO investors cancer will be a 'relic of the past' in ...
Article Text:
Dario Amodei’s cancer promise meets doctors’ doubts

Doctors say curing cancer and Alzheimer's in 10 years is not possible

Anthropic's case rests on WHO work, Claude Science and its own lab

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

In August, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei posted on X that saying AI will cure cancer "is more a cliché than it is inspiring, and most people think it is deceptive." The best way to win over sceptics, he added, was to "actually cure cancer. " Three months later, with Anthropic courting investors ahead of its Nasdaq listing, Amodei has made that very promise. In the company's IPO roadshow video, released on November 10, he said cancer, Alzheimer's, heart disease and mental illness will be "relics of the past" in less than a decade. Doctors, including Germany's former health minister Karl Lauterbach, are not buying the timeline."You know, if today we look at things like cancer, Alzheimer's, heart disease, mental illness, these will be relics of the past in, I think, less than a decade," Amodei said. He spoke of an "age of miracles" and tied it to safety, saying the company that gets the risks right will earn "the license to operate that society trusts."Anthropic is seeking a valuation of $1.4 trillion, and its shares are due to start trading on November 19.Lauterbach, a doctor and epidemiologist, responded in German on X on November 11. "It is unclear whether people like @DarioAmodei know so little about medicine or are deliberately misleading the public," he wrote.AI can help with cancer, Alzheimer's and mental illness, he said, but a cure "cannot possibly happen in just 10 years." He wants the focus on prevention.Melinda B. Chu, a doctor and AI medical researcher at Saint Louis University, said Anthropic "has done nothing to suggest they themselves will contribute meaningfully to these goals." Biotech executive Rami Elghandour was blunter about the setting. "I've taken two companies public. These are insane things to say in an IPO pitch," he said.The company's own letter to investors lists "underpromise and overdeliver" among its guiding principles.The same letter makes a softer claim. The seven co-founders wrote that AI could "bring cures for major diseases within reach." The WHO's Regional Office for Africa used Claude during the 2026 Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, cutting its daily situation report from a full day to under an hour. With the Gates Foundation, Anthropic backs free AI clinical search for doctors in about 100 low- and middle-income countries. The founders also say Claude can cut the time to write clinical trial reports "from months to minutes."Its Claude Science beta app for researchers runs analyses and queries more than 60 scientific databases. On the product page, UCSF principal investigator Stephen Francis says it found a lab virus contaminant in his team's RNA-seq data, a problem they had chased for most of a year.The company is building its own biology work too. In October, it bought a one-person biotech start-up working on muscular dystrophy and said it had "begun drug discovery efforts of our own." It reportedly runs a wet lab in the Bay Area.None of this touches the slowest part of medicine. AI can speed up screening molecules and picking drug candidates, but a new drug still has to clear safety, dosing and large efficacy trials in humans before regulators sign off. That part moves at the speed of human biology.Amodei set the bar himself in August. Sceptics will come round when cancer is actually cured, and that is one result no roadshow video can deliver.
Article Summary: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei says AI will cure cancer in less than a decade. Doctors, including Germany's former health minister Karl Lauterbach, are not buying the timeline. Anthropic is seeking a valuation of $1.4 trillion and its shares are due to start trading on November 19.

Article Title: US government to designate Nvidia, Microsoft, Amazon and 21 other companies as 'National Champions'; and the 'target' is again China
Article Text:
US government to designate Nvidia, Microsoft, Amazon and 21 other companies as 'National Champions'; and the 'target' is again China

What ‘National Champions’ designation will mean

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Jensen Huang ’s affair fuels fresh concerns

US government is planning to designate Nvidia, Microsoft, Amazon , OpenAI, Anthropic and 20 other companies as ‘National Champions’, and the ‘target’ is once again China. Citing sources familiar with the matter, Wall Street Journal reports that the program aims to get foreign companies and countries to adopt US AI technology over Chinese rivals. “The goal of the program is to package U.S. chips, models and other AI products so it is easy for customers in other countries to purchase them together,” the report said. According to it, the announcement is likely to come next week. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is expected to announce the plan, the people told the publication.WSJ states that the program was previously talked about a year ago. However, it was not then named ‘National Champions’. With the designation, nearly a dozen companies will be able to get expedited approvals for licenses to export chips and other technology, government support for their work overseas and access to federal financing.Sources told the publication that among the companies set to be named national champions are Nvidia, Amazon, Microsoft, OpenAI and Anthropic.The planned announcement comes amid renewed scrutiny of Nvidia following reports about its former CEO Jensen Huang’s alleged relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based data-center company Megaspeed.The WSJ reported that Alice Huang is suspected by US intelligence officials of being a Chinese intelligence source.The revelations have fueled calls from national security hawks to prioritise security concerns over market share, including through tighter restrictions on chip exports. Nvidia’s chips power some of the world’s most advanced AI models and are considered critical to the global AI industry.US President Donald Trump has repeatedly praised Jensen Huang for building a major American technology company that has become central to the AI boom.
Article Summary: US government to designate Nvidia, Microsoft, Amazon and 21 other companies as 'National Champions'; and the 'target' is again China. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is expected to announce the plan next week. With the designation, nearly a dozen companies will be able to get expedited approvals for licenses to export chips and other technology.

Article Title: A Google datacenter planned on 282 acres in Michigan has moved into construction despite local opposition; the project could use up to 3.6 million gallons of water a day and around one gigawatt of pow
Article Text:
Construction moves ahead after zoning approval

Approvals

Residents push back

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Multi-billion-dollar investment

Google has started construction on a massive hyperscale data centre in Michigan, moving ahead with the project despite months of opposition from local residents concerned about its environmental impact, water consumption and energy demands. According to a report by Mlive, the facility called ‘Project Cannoli’ is planned on a 282-acre site in Van Buren Township near Detroit Metro Airport. The datacenter project is said to become one of the largest investments made by Google in the region. The report further states that the datacenter could consume up to 3.6 million gallons of water per day and need around one gigawatt of electricity when it will become fully functional. This energy consumption of the data centre has raised concerns among the residents, as it will create a lot of pressure on local infrastructure.The development cleared a key hurdle in October when the Van Buren Township Planning Commission voted 5-1 to approve the final site plan. Officials noted that the site was already zoned for industrial use and that planning commissioners were required to approve projects that complied with zoning regulations.The proposed facility will be located between Interstate 94 and Interstate 275, a few miles west of Detroit Metropolitan Airport. The land currently consists of fields, woodland and wetlands. Google will ultimately own and operate the facility, while industrial developer Panattoni is overseeing construction.On October 14, the Van Buren Township Planning Commission voted 5-1 to approve the final site plan after nearly an hour of public comment. The site is already zoned industrial, and the board must approve projects that meet those guidelines. Commissioner Jeff Jahr said the board’s job was to verify the construction is in line with the law. Officials from the township and Wayne County agreed to a $125 million tax break for the project, and county commissioners overrode a veto by County Executive Warren Evans in early October to approve it. The tax break halves local taxes and is worth an estimated $125 million over 12 years. In return, Google will pay the township $15.4 million for local infrastructure and guarantee at least 51 full-time jobs. Google will own and operate the site, and the industrial developer Panattoni is managing construction. Walbridge, a Detroit-based contractor, will build it. Panattoni says the project would bring $2 billion in contracts to Wayne County businesses and 50 to 200 on-site jobs.Residents, especially those in an adjacent subdivision, have objected to noise, utility use and construction impacts. Neighbours say early construction is already affecting them through noise and dust. At the October meeting, resident Maggie Brumar said she hears dump trucks unloading every half hour and can’t keep her windows open because of dust. Others have been angrier. Joe Jones said it was misguided to expect Google to bring benefits to the community.Opposition has also turned political. It has sparked a recall effort targeting the entire township board. Supporters, including the Detroit Regional Partnership, say Google would become the township’s largest taxpayer and pay for public services. Local food pantry operator Mickie Wordhouse said she hoped the project would lead to better public services.Supporters of the project have described it as a once-in-a-generation economic opportunity for the region. Panattoni executives told local officials that construction activities alone would generate about $2 billion in contracts for Wayne County businesses. The completed facility is expected to employ between 50 and 200 on-site workers.Google also received significant local incentives. Wayne County and Van Buren Township approved a tax incentive package worth approximately $125 million after county commissioners voted to override a veto from Wayne County Executive Warren Evans. Google has agreed to contribute $15 million each to the county and township as part of the arrangement. Economic development officials have argued that the arrival of Google could make the company the township's largest taxpayer and generate substantial revenue for local public services.
Article Summary: The facility called ‘Project Cannoli’ is planned on a 282-acre site in Van Buren Township near Detroit Metro Airport. The datacenter project is said to become one of the largest investments made by Google in the region. It could consume up to 3.6 million gallons of water per day and need around one gigawatt of electricity when it will become fully functional.

Apple Intelligence features beyond Siri AI

Siri AI usage limits and what Apple plans to charge

Siri on the Mac has always been the version people forget is there, tucked into a menu bar icon most users click once and never again. The rebuilt assistant that arrived with macOS 27 Golden Gate on September 14 goes after that problem from a different angle, by putting itself inside Spotlight, inside the Control-click menu and behind a screenshot shortcut. The fastest way to reach Siri AI on a desktop now involves no talking at all.Mac owners also got a break nobody else did. Apple has withheld Siri AI from iPhone, iPad and Apple Watch across the European Union, yet Macs are carved out of that restriction. An EU account on macOS 27 Golden Gate can run the assistant provided the system language and Siri language are both English. Accounts registered in mainland China remain locked out on every device Apple sells.Switching it on is quick, but finishing the setup does not mean you can use it yet:The last of those puts you on a waitlist and the download begins on its own once you clear it. Apple gives no estimate for the wait, and reports since launch have swung between a few minutes and most of an afternoon. Running Apple Intelligence before you upgraded buys you nothing here, because that earlier consent does not carry over.Two lines cover eligibility. The A18 Pro MacBook Neo qualifies, and so does any Mac running M1 or newer.Intel machines are out, with no beta workaround.Underneath that sits a narrower requirement most people miss. Expressive voices, the setting that lets you dial Siri's pace and expressiveness, needs AFM Core Advanced, Apple's newest on-device model. On the Mac that translates to an M3 chip or later with at least 12GB of unified memory. An M1 MacBook Air will run the assistant fine and never see those controls.Language is the other limit. English is all Siri AI speaks for now, with French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese and Spanish due next month, and both your system language and Siri language have to match a supported option.Most of the Mac-specific engineering has gone into access points rather than fresh abilities:Driving all of this is a new generation of Apple Foundation Models that the company says was built with Google, using its Gemini models. Requests are split between the Mac and Private Cloud Compute, where Apple's stated position is that personal data is never retained and stays out of reach of its own staff.Photos adds Spatial Reframing, an Extend tool and a rebuilt Clean Up. Image Playground handles photorealistic output now and accepts edits by description, with SynthID watermarking due in a later release. Safari sorts tabs into topics by itself, tracks pages for restocks or price cuts through Notify Me, and assembles custom extensions from a written brief. Shortcuts takes the same route to automations, and Calendar accepts plain-language changes to events.Anything routed through Apple's servers, Siri AI included, draws on a daily allowance. The company has declined to publish a number, saying the ceiling moves with the feature, the complexity of the request and how loaded the system is at the time.What Apple has committed to is charging for expanded access at some point. There is no price, no date, and no indication of whether the current free allowance survives once that tier exists.
Article Summary: Siri on the Mac has always been the version people forget is there, tucked into a menu bar icon most users click once and never again. The rebuilt assistant that arrived with macOS 27 Golden Gate on September 14 goes after that problem from a different angle, by putting itself inside Spotlight, inside the Control- click menu and behind a screenshot shortcut. The fastest way to reach Siri AI on a desktop now involves no talking at all.

Article Title: Ukraine President Zelenskyy makes another Starlink complaint; says: 'Detected speed restrictions on Starshield'; Spacex responds
Article Text:

Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is upset again with Spacex Starlink. At a public function in Europe, Zelensky reportedly claimed that Starshield has again been disabled on fast-moving drones in Ukrainian territory occupied by Russian forces. For those unaware, Starshield is the military variant of Spacex's Starlink satellite service."We have detected speed restrictions on Starshield on our Ukrainian territory again, in the temporarily occupied parts of Ukraine," Zelenskyy said in a speech at the 9th European Political Community Summit in Ireland. “The speed limit is back at 161 kilometers per hour—that’s 100 miles per hour.” According to him, Starshield stops working on Ukrainian military drones when they travel above 161 kilometers per hour.Zelenskyy added that Ukraine doesn’t know why the limit is in place again. “We are trying to get the details from the American side, but so far we know very little,” Zelenskyy said. “But some things are very clear. If someone in America is making decisions that basically treat Ukrainian territory as if it is not Ukrainian, then this tells us where things are going. We need to be clear and never recognize Russia’s occupation of Ukrainian territory in any way.Speed restrictions hurting us, claims Zelenskyy“This directly affects our ability to intercept Russian jet-powered Shahed drones,” Zelenskyy said. “These drones come from those [occupied] areas, and because of the speed restrictions, we simply cannot catch up with them in time. Near the front line, we cannot use our aircraft. Only drone interceptors can operate there. And without the speed we need, shooting down these Shaheds becomes much harder. This means more Russian strikes get through, and more of our people are killed, our civilians are killed, by Russia. ”This is the second time in less than a month that Ukraine is making such allegations. Last month too, Ukraine claimed that Starlink terminals used by Ukrainian drone units began experiencing signal failures at speeds above 160 km/h, disrupting several missions early on Wednesday morning, according to military personnel and senior Ukrainian officials.Ukraine officials reportedly said that they believe the limit was reinstated to put pressure on Ukraine in the latest round of peace talks with Russia. Zelenskyy said that without satellite connectivity on its drones, Ukraine cannot intercept Russian drones that fly in from the occupied parts of Ukraine. The Starlink disruption, it was claimed, comes as Kyiv faces escalating Russian attacks on its energy infrastructure and mounting pressure from US President Donald Trump to make concessions to Moscow to end the war.Spacex rejects Zelenskyy's claimsOn its part, SpaceX rejected Zelenskyy's allegation. Spacex's media relations department told Ars Technica when asked about Zelenskyy’s statement that Starshield is being restricted again. “This is false. There has been no change,” said the spokesperson.Spacex has received multiple Pentagon contracts to give Ukraine access to Starshield. In October, Spacex CEO Elon Musk said that any decisions on Starshield restrictions are made by the US government. The Pentagon inspector general’s office has since declined a request from US senators to investigate who ordered the restrictions.
Article Summary: Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is upset again with Spacex Starlink. He claims that Starshield has again been disabled on fast-moving drones in Ukrainian territory occupied by Russian forces. According to him, Starsh yield stops working on Ukrainian military drones when they travel above 161 kilometers per hour.

Article Title: Logitech gives 7,000 employees an extra paid day off to play GTA 6 or any other video games; company says: The time employees spend playing will…
Article Text:
GTA 6 is days away, and Logitech has told 7,000 employees to take a paid day off and play

Logitech says its own research shows gaming helps at work

GTA 6 release on November 19 has employers bracing for empty desks

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Logitech has given its 7,000 employees worldwide an extra paid day off to play video games, so nobody has to fake a sick day. Called Logi Game Day, the perk covers everyone from full-time staff to interns. It arrives less than a week before Grand Theft Auto 6 hits PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series consoles on November 19.The day doesn't have to be spent in Vice City, either. Employees can pick any title they like and take the day off anytime until November 2027. "We believe that the time employees spend playing will enhance the time they spend working," said Robin Piispanen, general manager of Logitech G, the company's gaming brand.CEO Hanneke Faber is pitching it as a push against an old idea. "It's time to retire the stereotype that gaming is a waste of time," she said, adding that as a company making products for both work and play, Logitech sees "how engagement in one sphere supports performance in the other."Piispanen, a former competitive gamer, put it more simply: "We know excellence doesn't come from constant grinding. It comes from having space to recharge and have fun."The company is backing the idea with its own numbers. In its Ctrl Tomorrow study, 81% of gamers said playing builds real-world confidence, eases anxiety and goes hand in hand with better day-to-day work performance. A separate survey found 98.8% of enterprise IT decision-makers believe skills like problem-solving and staying calm under pressure carry over to work.The leadership is on board too. Chief financial officer Matteo Anversa plans to spend his day on Forza with a simulation racing rig, while chief people officer Elaine Laird already has a running Block Blast rivalry with coworkers. "Play is not the opposite of work," Laird said. Elsewhere in the company, one manager plans to settle "household disputes" with her husband in Call of Duty, and an electrical engineer has Elden Ring lined up.The perk arrives as employers brace for a mass no-show. GTA 6 is the first new entry in the series in 13 years, after GTA 5 sold over 235 million units. José García Montalvo, an economics professor at Pompeu Fabra University in Barcelona, estimates that up to 1.5 million US workers could skip work on release day, costing the economy around $1 billion in lost productivity. Economist Victor Matheson of the College of the Holy Cross has questioned the figure, arguing that most of those missed hours will simply be made up later in the year.HR software firm BambooHR says time-off requests for November 19 are 9% to 17% higher than on a typical third Thursday in November. Logitech isn't the only one planning around it. A US Army battalion in Georgia is offering soldiers who reenlist a four-day pass, and a few smaller firms are shutting for the day.Faber will spend November 19 at Logitech's San Jose office, which is being turned into a gaming lounge for a streamed event hosted by Piispanen. "I'm ready for some fun and (friendly) competition," she said.
Article Summary: Logitech has given its 7,000 employees worldwide an extra paid day off to play video games. The perk covers everyone from full-time staff to interns. It arrives less than a week before Grand Theft Auto 6 hits PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series consoles on November 19.

There's another twist in Nvidia founder Jensen Huang's romantic relationship with Alice Huang. In a statement, Singapore-based company Megaspeed said that Alice Huang, whose ties to ‌former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang raised US national security concerns, had officially left the company on August 30, 2025, ⁠and that she has no current role at the Singapore-based company. “Ms. Alice Huang officially left Megaspeed effective August 30, 2025 and currently has no role with the Company,” Megaspeed said in an emailed statement shared with CNBC. “Megaspeed does not comment on Ms. Huang’s personal and private matters,” it added.The statement comes after reports linked Nvidia founder and then CEO Jensen Huang to Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive. Article Title: How Bees helped engineers solve what has been regarded as Solar panels’ biggest flaw since invention; and has been a major waste of energy
Article Text:
Representative image

Why angled sunlight creates a problem for solar panels

How honeycomb geometry gives light another chance

Why engineers turned to the structure of a beehive

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Bees have inspired engineers to rethink solar panel design. The honeycomb structure behind their hives has provided a blueprint for tackling a persistent problem: sunlight reflecting away from panels instead of generating electricity. Conventional flat panels receive sunlight more directly around midday, but the sun's changing angle affects how much light they capture.Engineers have developed a concave, three-dimensional design that redirects reflected light towards another surface, giving it a second chance to be absorbed. According to a report by The Pulse, the honeycomb-inspired structure increased maximum power output by 142.3% compared with a flat panel under the same conditions, offering a way to reduce wasted sunlight without tracking motors.Traditional solar panels have a flat surface. As the sun moves across the sky, its rays strike that surface at different angles. When sunlight arrives at an oblique angle, reflection from the protective glass becomes a problem. Light that bounces away cannot contribute to the panel’s electricity output.The honeycomb-inspired design changes the path of that reflected light. Rather than relying on a single flat surface, it uses sloping surfaces arranged into concave structures.Inside the three-dimensional module, sunlight can strike one slanted wall and bounce towards the opposite wall. Instead of immediately escaping, the reflected light encounters another surface where it can be absorbed. This process, described as enhanced light recapture, is central to the design.The supplied material reports a maximum power output increase of 142.3% over a conventional flat panel. At a zero-degree angle, when sunlight strikes directly, output increased by 36.4%. At 60 degrees, the reported improvement was 61.8%.These figures describe increases in power output under the stated comparison conditions, rather than the proportion of sunlight converted into electricity.Honeycomb combines closely packed hexagonal cells with strength and efficient material use. Engineers used this natural geometry as the basis for their solar module.Tilting the walls creates small valleys that help retain light within the structure. The benefit comes from how those surfaces redirect sunlight, allowing neighbouring surfaces to capture photons that might otherwise escape.To support the arrangement, engineers developed a flexible, printed polymer mechanical metamaterial, which is a structure whose engineered pattern helps determine its mechanical behaviour.The flexible backing could extend the design beyond flat rooftops. The report identifies curved walls, electric vehicles and aerospace equipment as potential applications.Its ability to fit curved surfaces could allow solar modules to be incorporated into places where conventional flat panels are difficult to install.
Article Summary: Engineers have developed a concave, three-dimensional design that redirects reflected light towards another surface, giving it a second chance to be absorbed. The honeycomb-inspired structure increased maximum power output by 142.3% compared with a flat panel under the same conditions.

Article Title: Darrell Dai, a robot research engineer at Nvidia resigns; complains to Nvidia board: You did not hear engineers working in the company on Jensen Huang, we also have a 'story to tell'
Article Text:
Darrell Dai, a robot research engineer at Nvidia resigns; complains to Nvidia board: You did not hear engineers working in the company on Jensen Huang, we also have a 'story to tell'

Here’s the post shared by Nvidia robot research engineer

"I’ve decided to leave NVIDIA. There are a few things I want to say.

As a robotics engineer at NVIDIA, I have seen Jensen as much more than the company’s CEO.

I admire his willingness to invest in a future that was not yet obvious. He committed to CUDA long before the deep learning boom and positioned NVIDIA for AI before it became everyone’s priority. Those decisions helped build the infrastructure that powers today’s AI.

I have seen that same vision in physical AI: investing in robotics, sharing open-source tools and projects, and building computing platforms that bring AI into the physical world. This is the work I do every day—and a future I believe in.

But what matters most to me is the culture he helped build.

Engineers are encouraged to explore, take risks, and learn from mistakes. Jensen reads employees’ Top 5 emails, follows their work, and engages directly.

In a company this large, that connection matters. It makes an individual engineer feel that their ideas can still be heard.

That is why this has been so disappointing.

I do not have all the facts surrounding the allegations, and I cannot prejudge the investigation. My admiration for Jensen does not put him above scrutiny.

What I find difficult to accept is having to come to terms with his departure before receiving an explanation that helps me understand it.

What this means for our direction, our culture, and the people doing the work remains unclear to me.

I have felt that engineers’ perspectives matter here. On this decision, I have not felt heard. That gap has been more painful than I expected.

When life gets too busy and chaotic, it is tempting to postpone a task or ignore piling problems but according to Amazon founder Jeff Bezos , dodging the issue is exactly what keeps anxiety alive. Bezos has shared a straightforward rule for handling pressure: take action. With a net worth of $361 billion, the world’s second-richest man knows a thing or two about high-stakes pressure, and coming from Bezos means the advice is likely right.“I find if I’m stressed about something it’s usually because I’m not doing anything about it. I’m listening to my body as a signal that something is wrong, and I find that the stress goes away the second I take the first step,” Bezos said during a 2017 visit to the Museum of Flight in Seattle. Long before Amazon became the No. 1 Fortune 500 company, Bezos launched it out of a rented garage and had to sit through 60 meetings just to raise his first $1 million in seed capital in the mid-1990s.Instead of letting stress paralyse him, Bezos uses it as a diagnostic tool. “If I’m stressed about something, I’m trying to figure out why [I am] stressed. I’m listening to my body as a signal,” he said. Once he identifies the problem, his next move is to bring other people into the room.Talking things through and collaborating with allies, he explained, can turn an overwhelming situation into something enjoyable.“If you can find friends who are interested in similar things or want to help you solve a problem, problem-solving is inspiring for me all by itself. There’s nothing more fun than getting in a room with a group of inventors and saying: ‘Look, here’s the problem. Let’s invent a solution to it.’ And as soon as you start doing that, I find that it turns from something that might create stress into something that creates fun,” Bezos said.Inside Amazon, executives also lean on Bezos’s 16 leadership principles when navigating tough calls. “The leadership principles are something you have to constantly work at. When they’re applied well, they’re powerful,” Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said in the company’s Leadership Principles Explained video series.While Bezos prefers to push straight through adversity, other chief executives rely on different habits to keep stress in check. For Satya Nadella (Microsoft), facing challenges head-on is the key but he focuses heavily on preventing employee burnout through open dialogue and flexible workplace policies.“The notion of having work-life harmony in a highly competitive economy is a first-class topic. You cannot have people burn out. It’s bad for your company, and it’s bad for society,” Nadella once said, as per Fortune.Laxman Narasimhan (Former Starbucks CEO), Narasimhan told Fortune in a 2023 interview that he relies on three strict “nonnegotiables” to avoid burnout: daily meditation, regular exercise, and protected family time. “I’m very disciplined about balance,” he said.

Dario Amodei's Anthropic has pledged $50 million to support Bay Area nonprofits through the end of 2027, its largest philanthropic commitment to its hometown region. The San Francisco-based artificial intelligence company will start with $500,000 in holiday grants to help provide groceries, free meals, shelter and toys for children.Anthropic is setting up a donor-advised fund with the San Francisco Foundation. The company will select future recipients with guidance from the foundation. Grants will be awarded by invitation.The announcement came on the same day Anthropic set pricing for an initial public offering (IPO) that could value it at up to $1.4 trillion. The pledge amounts to about 0.0036% of that potential valuation. It also comes as rising food and housing costs put pressure on Bay Area households and local tech leaders face calls to give more. A day earlier, Airbnb CEO Brian Chesky donated $100 million to support San Francisco parks."San Francisco has always been a place of enormous possibility, but that possibility isn’t shared equally by everyone. We have been privileged to build Anthropic here, and we want to make sure our success expands opportunity, not widens the gaps that already exist. That’s why we’re partnering with the San Francisco Foundation, whose deep knowledge of the Bay Area will help guide this commitment to where it’s needed most,” said Daniela Amodei, Co-founder and President of Anthropic.The initial $500,000 will go to the San Francisco-Marin Food Bank, Glide Memorial Church, the Interfaith Winter Shelter and San Francisco Firefighters Local 798’s Toy Program. The food bank works with 265 community organisations to reach more than 46,000 households each week across San Francisco and Marin counties. Glide, which has operated in San Francisco’s Tenderloin since 1963, serves three free meals a day year-round and provides assistance to families.The Interfaith Winter Shelter, founded by the San Francisco Interfaith Council, has for more than three decades united over 50 faith communities to welcome neighbors in from the cold with a warm bed, a hot meal, and a shower, so they can rest and plan their next step.San Francisco has been home to Anthropic co-founders Dario and Daniela Amodei since childhood; both attended Lowell High School. They later started Anthropic in their hometown, with early employees gathering in Precita Park to map out a vision for safer AI systems. Today, the company has more than 2,500 employees at its San Francisco headquarters, and its Claude chatbot is widely used by local businesses and nonprofits.Fred Blackwell, chief executive of the San Francisco Foundation, said Anthropic approached the organisation just over a week before the announcement and wanted to get money to local groups quickly. He described the pledge as one of the largest corporate donations in the foundation’s history. "Where you live matters, and so does what you put into it. The Bay Area has always been a place where people build big things. That should include building strong communities. Anthropic is making a real commitment to the place it calls home, and we hope others are inspired to do the same. That’s how the whole region thrives,” said Fred Blackwell, CEO, San Francisco Foundation.Blackwell pointed to federal healthcare cuts, local government budget deficits and high prices for food, housing and childcare as pressures on Bay Area residents. He said the foundation was having one of its strongest fundraising years in recent memory and hoped Anthropic’s pledge would encourage other companies to give.

Facebook and Instagram parent Meta has been fined in Italy. Italian regulators have fined the social media giant Meta $887 million for accessing Android smartphone users' photos and videos without their specific consent. The Italian regulator said that the company had accessed Android users' photographs and videos without obtaining their consent or informing them. The fine is among the largest an Italian authority has ever imposed on a technology company.Italy's Data Protection Authority said that Meta did not properly inform about 20 million smartphone users that it had access to their photos and videos via a feature of the Facebook app.In its order, the regulator has given Meta 60 days to disable the feature by default and seek users' consent separately for access.The charge is related to a feature which suggests photos and videos from a user's phone gallery as ideas for posts. Facebook requested access to users' photo galleries through a single app-wide authorisation. According to the Italian regulator, a preceding notice did not make clear that this would also allow Facebook to generate suggestions based on photos in users' phone gallery.The regulator said that it took into account "the high number of people affected" and the fact it is "still ongoing for those who have not updated the app and for those who have already given their consent to the system".It also cited "Meta's lack of co-operation". The investigation, ‌which ⁠began in 2025, did not cover the possible use of the content to train artificial intelligence models, a practice Meta denied, ​the authority ​said. It added ⁠that it reserved the right to assess separately a new ​feature, launched in 2026, that allows ​content ⁠from users' galleries to be processed in the cloudIn October, Meta was hit with its largest fine ever for its business practices. A US judge in New Mexico ordered the company to pay $25 billion after it found that it had spent years lying to the public about how it handled Facebook user data.The ruling came in ‌a case related to allegations that Cambridge Analytica, a British political consulting company involved in Donald Trump's 2016 presidential campaign, obtained data from millions of Facebook users without their consent. New Mexico had sued Meta, accusing it of lying to Facebook users in New Mexico about who had access to their data. "Facebook's wrongdoing — over the course of years and systematically broadcast to the public — goes to the heart of Facebook's core business practices," Judge ​Francis Mathew wrote in his order, which came more than three weeks after the verdict.

Article Title: A Maryland county used AI cameras on school buses to generate 375,000 tickets and $92 million in fines; investigation finds little change in the violations they were meant to reduce

How the camera programme is funded

How AI cameras identify suspected violations

Montgomery County’s school bus cameras are facing questions over safety. The Maryland county issued more than 375,000 tickets and $92 million in fines through its camera enforcement programme, but an investigation by Bloomberg Businessweek and Type Investigations found little reduction in violations and no evidence of fewer collisions near stopped school buses.The findings raise questions about whether the programme is changing driver behaviour. BusPatrol, which operates the cameras, says its technology helps protect children while allowing local authorities to fund installation and operations through violation revenue. Its artificial intelligence cameras flag suspected illegal passing, but police review the evidence before issuing tickets. The $92 million represents fines issued, rather than money collected.County figures cited in the investigation show that citations per active camera fell only slightly, from 36 in 2020 to 34 in 2025. Total citations increased over that period, from 50,698 to 51,779.The investigation examined county records, local news reports and camera footage. Its finding of no evidence of fewer collisions does not establish that cameras have no safety value, but it questions whether the volume of tickets demonstrates the promised improvement.Between fiscal years 2019 and 2024, Montgomery County retained about $18.5 million from collected fines while setting aside roughly $40 million for BusPatrol, according to the investigation.BusPatrol says its financial arrangements allow it to recover installation and operating costs. The company also says it covers the shortfall when camera expenses exceed violation revenue.The model allows school districts to install equipment without paying the full cost upfront. However, the investigation found that technology fees and revenue-sharing arrangements can leave participating authorities with a limited share of the proceeds.The cameras record vehicles suspected of illegally passing stopped school buses. BusPatrol packages the evidence for police review, with officers deciding whether a citation should follow.The distinction matters because an AI-generated flag is not a finding that a driver broke the law. Human review is still part of the enforcement process.At the time of the investigation, BusPatrol had equipped about 35,000 buses in 24 states and more than 350 school districts. The company said its systems promote student safety and driver accountability and that official crash statistics don't account for near misses.
Article Summary: Montgomery County issued more than 375,000 tickets and $92 million in fines. Investigation found little reduction in violations and no evidence of fewer collisions near stopped school buses. BusPatrol, which operates the cameras, says its technology helps protect children while allowing local authorities to fund installation and operations.

Big tech companies, including Google, Microsoft, Amazon and others rode the artificial intelligence (AI) boom to record highs. But spooked investors are pulling back even as billions of dollars vanish from the market value of major IT giants. Now, one veteran executive says his company is built to weather whatever comes next: Michael Dell. The company he started in a college dorm room in 1984 with $1,000 has evolved from selling direct-to-consumer PCs into supplying the massive AI supercomputers tech giants are scrambling to buy. Thanks to a projected 70% jump in revenue for its current fiscal year, Dell Technologies’ valuation is now nearly four times what it was a year ago.While hyperscalers like Amazon and Google – along with AI data-center builders known as neoclouds, such as CoreWeave, Nebius and Crusoe – are taking on heavy debt to fund their AI hubs, Dell is playing a very different financial game, as per a recent report by The Wall Street Journal.When asked how he is preparing for a potential downturn in the AI cycle, Dell pointed straight to his balance sheet: “There are some new challenges that this presents, but if you look at our cash conversion cycle, it’s still negative.”Essentially, Dell relies on just-in-time manufacturing. It only builds its powerful AI servers and PCs after a customer places an order. By collecting payments from buyers upfront and taking longer to pay its own vendors, Dell sits on that cash for days or even weeks. That gives the company a healthy financial cushion and protects it from getting stuck with warehouses full of unsold hardware if demand suddenly dries up.For now, Dell says business is humming. Even with stiff competition from Super Micro, HPE and Lenovo, Dell leads the pack in supplying the computing brains for enterprises building their own AI. It took Dell eight quarters to sign up 3,200 customers building AI data centers with its servers, a list that includes Elon Musk’s SpaceX. In just the last three quarters, it added another 3,300.Right now, Dell is sitting on $95 billion in back-orders for its AI server racks – massive machines that weigh 3,000 pounds each and draw as much electricity as 100 or more typical US homes. The real hurdle isn’t finding buyers; it is getting enough memory chips to actually build and ship the machines. Looking ahead to next year, Dell offered a blunt assessment of the supply crunch: “It’s gonna get worse.”Dell isn't the only executive who lived through the dot-com bust and is now structuring his business to survive a potential AI pullback. Wendell Weeks, the CEO of Corning, a company whose stock and revenue soared during the dot-com era before crashing alongside the fiber-optic build-out, has adopted a similar playbook. Corning has struck deals with Nvidia, Amazon and Meta Platforms where those tech giants help pay to expand Corning's fiber-optics manufacturing capacity.As the longest-serving CEO of any Fortune 500 company and one of the wealthiest people in the world, Dell has become a central figure in the AI era. He has been gifted a signed AI server by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, earned a shout-out from Elon Musk on X for touring a SpaceX data-center site in a hard hat, and recently received a medal at the White House from President Trump alongside Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and Google co-founder Sergey Brin.
Article Summary: Michael Dell started Dell Technologies in a college dorm room in 1984 with $1,000. Dell now supplies the massive AI supercomputers tech giants are scrambling to buy. Dell relies on just-in-time manufacturing and only builds its powerful AI servers and PCs after a customer places an order.

Article Title: Russian billionaire’s $600 million high-tech superyacht, dubbed ugliest in the world, is ‘stuck’ in Italy; it takes $11 million a year to keep its systems running
Article Text:
Sailing Yacht A has been docked in Trieste since Italy seized it in March 2022

Super-yacht needs $30,000 per day just to sit in port

Why Italy can’t switch off the air conditioning

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Italian authorities have reportedly been stuck with an unusual and expensive responsibility for more than four years: paying to keep a Russian billionaire’s $600 million superyacht in pristine condition. Sailing Yacht A, owned by Russian industrialist Andrey Melnichenko who has brought in new technologies in his businesses, has been sitting in the port of Trieste since March 2022, when Italian authorities seized it under international sanctions. Even though the futuristic vessel cannot leave the dock, it still requires constant maintenance, a working crew and nonstop power.Even worse for Italy’s budget, authorities cannot simply shut the ship down to save money. Inside the yacht sits a multimillion-euro private art collection, including paintings by Claude Monet, that would deteriorate if the air conditioning were turned off.According to the French newspaper Le Parisien, keeping Sailing Yacht A, reportedly dubbed the world’s ugliest superyacht, in working order costs roughly $30,000 a day, or nearly $11 million a year. That money pays for a 20-person skeleton crew tasked with cleaning the vessel and running its onboard systems, along with specialized upkeep, insurance, climate control and fuel.Sailing Yacht A is powered by four variable-speed generators, each capable of producing 2,800 kW, for a combined capacity of 11.2 megawatts. Depending on the ship's power needs at any given moment, those generators burn through roughly 400 gallons of diesel every hour to run essential machinery and protect the interiors from decay.The financial headache could soon get much worse. A report published in July noted that Italy may have to spend another $12 million on the yacht as it nears a mandatory class-renewal survey. While the initial certification costs far less, the technical repairs required to pass inspection could run into the millions – a bill the Italian Treasury might have to advance.The strangest part of the maintenance bill is hidden inside the ship. In January 2023, an investigation by the Italian television program Le Iene revealed that Sailing Yacht A holds at least eight paintings, including works by Claude Monet and other Impressionists, as well as pieces by 17th- and 18th-century French artists.A regional fine-arts official who inspected the collection explained that the paintings require stable temperatures to survive. As canvas, wooden supports and layers of paint react differently to moisture, swinging temperatures and humidity can cause surfaces to warp, crack and flake. Too much humidity also invites mold and condensation behind the frames.As a result, the yacht’s climate-control systems are a preservation necessity. Switching off the power to save on diesel could trigger far more expensive damage to the artwork.The yacht features three massive masts, eight decks, multiple elevators and suspended spiral staircases. Its interiors are outfitted with dark wood, copper accents, patterned carpets, integrated bookcases, and a multilevel main salon.
Article Summary: Sailing Yacht A, owned by Russian industrialist Andrey Melnichenko, has been docked in Trieste since March 2022. The superyacht requires constant maintenance, a working crew and nonstop power. Even worse for Italy’s budget, authorities cannot simply shut the ship down to save money. Inside the yacht sits a multimillion-euro private art collection, including paintings by Claude Monet.

Article Title: As cannabis prices crash, US growers look to AI data centres for a way out; city council member says: I’m OK with exploring that option, but...
Article Text:
As cannabis prices crash, US growers look to AI data centres for a way out; city council member says: I’m OK with exploring that option, but...

Why cannabis farms could be used for AI data centres

City council member is open to the idea, but has concerns

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Struggling cannabis farmers in the US may see some respite, thanks to AI data centres. According to Arizona Public Media report, Moe Asnani, a weed business owner has set his sights on a new project: converting old cannabis farms into mini data centers. The idea comes as cannabis growers face falling prices, rising costs and increased competition. In Arizona, cannabis sales peaked in 2024, with an oversupply of marijuana pushing prices down. As a result, some growers are considering selling their cultivation facilities or finding new uses for them.Asnani, the former owner of two D2 Dispensaries in Tucson, believes these facilities could be repurposed to support the growing demand for computing power.“For some reason, there's a lot more cannabis grown in Arizona than Arizonans use. And so, a lot of folks are getting out of that business, like myself, at least on the cultivation side. But these facilities can potentially be repurposed to be mini data center nodes,” he told Arizona Public Media.Indoor cannabis farms already require substantial amounts of electricity and water to support lighting, climate control and plant growth.These facilities may therefore have some of the infrastructure needed to run small data centres.Asnani's proposal is based on converting existing buildings rather than constructing entirely new facilities. The approach is known as “adaptive reuse”, in which an existing property is given a new purpose.The proposed mini data centres would be smaller than large facilities such as the Project Blue data centre being built near the Tucson fairgrounds.Asnani's former company, D2, estimated that its 18,000-square-foot cultivation facility used around 1.7 million gallons of water in 2024. For comparison, Project Blue could use up to 31 million gallons of water annually.However, existing infrastructure does not automatically make a cannabis farm suitable for a data centre. Operators would still need to assess power capacity, cooling systems, internet connectivity and other requirements.The proposal has caught the attention of Tucson City Council member Paul Cunningham, who said he is willing to explore the possibility of converting former cannabis facilities into data centres. “Data centers are dirty words and everybody knows that. And no one wants to build a brand new data center anywhere,” Cunningham said.“But if we have buildings that were using that amount of water and that amount of energy already in their previous function and [it] can be done without being invasive, I'm OK with exploring that option.”Asnani has another reason for pursuing the idea. He believes smaller data centres could help create what he calls “sovereign AI”, allowing users to control their own data processing rather than relying entirely on large technology companies.“The whole idea is if you create these smaller nodes where people control their own data, where they're not at the mercy of other people's updates and things like that — that's kind of where the idea came in, because I believe in decentralization,” he said.The concept could appeal to organisations looking for more local control over their computing infrastructure. However, smaller data centres are not automatically more secure than larger ones. Experts say cybersecurity depends on network safeguards and the people managing the systems.
Article Summary: Moe Asnani, former owner of two D2 Dispensaries in Tucson, has set his sights on a new project: converting old cannabis farms into mini data centres. The idea comes as cannabis growers face falling prices, rising costs and increased competition. In Arizona, cannabis sales peaked in 2024.

Article Title: Microsoft has an 'email warning' for its Outlook and Teams users after 24-hour-plus outage; says: Do not …

Microsoft has an 'email warning' for its Outlook and Teams users after 24-hour-plus outage; says: Do not …

Here’s what Microsoft said

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Microsoft has issued an email warning for Outlook and Teams users following a 24-hour-plus Microsoft 365 service disruption on November 12. In an X (formerly Twitter) post, the company said that cybercriminals are exploiting the outage to send phishing emails that impersonate official service health notifications. Some messages claim that emails held during the disruption will be deleted within 24 hours unless users click a link to restore them. Microsoft has urged organisations to verify service alerts through the Microsoft 365 admin centre and investigate suspicious emails. "Microsoft Threat Intelligence observed an active phishing campaign exploiting the Microsoft 365 service disruption on November 12. The messages impersonate Microsoft 365 service health notifications and reference the legitimate Exchange Online incident EX1550543," the post said."Organizations should verify their Safe Links policies, investigate potential user interactions, and confirm service disruptions directly through the Microsoft 365 admin center,” it stated.In the X post, Microsoft Threat Intelligence wrote:“Microsoft Threat Intelligence observed an active phishing campaign exploiting the Microsoft 365 service disruption on November 12. The messages impersonate Microsoft 365 service health notifications and reference the legitimate Exchange Online incident EX1550543.Some of the phishing emails Microsoft detected on November 13 falsely claim that messages were held during the outage and will be deleted within 24 hours unless recipients click to restore them.Observed subjects follow the pattern "Outage - [six-character code]," with sender display names using organization-specific prefixes followed by "Outage Notification" or "Service Health."The campaign uses three sender domains, moments-notice[.]com, planetmaison[.]com, and newbooker[.]com, with recipient-specific SendGrid click-tracking links redirecting to reallifeaccounting[.]com, including the observed path /themelist0.html. Similar messages targeted organizations across multiple US sectors.The activity is consistent with credential phishing, although credential collection and malware delivery have not been confirmed.Security teams can use Microsoft Defender for Office 365 Threat Explorer and Microsoft Defender XDR advanced hunting (EmailEvents, EmailUrlInfo, and UrlClickEvents) to identify suspicious messages, examine embedded URLs, and investigate user clicks.Microsoft Defender for Office 365 Safe Links provides time-of-click protection against malicious URLs when properly configured. Organizations should verify their Safe Links policies, investigate potential user interactions, and confirm service disruptions directly through the Microsoft 365 admin center.”

Article Title: How one network change disrupted Microsoft Outlook, Teams and the AI tools that rely on them
Article Text:
The same traffic, fewer servers

Poll Vote & Share your view Would you trust Microsoft services after this incident? Yes, absolutely No, not at all 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Why the outage reached Teams, ChatGPT and Claude

Microsoft's apology and a 'promise'

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A financial firm in Taiwan went back to the fax machine to confirm trades. At Europe’s Euronext exchange, email was disrupted. Shipping group Maersk warned customers that updates could take longer. The three businesses were among thousands of those caught up in a Microsoft outage that began on November 12 and took more than a day to ease. One of the world’s largest software companies had changed something in its network. A trading desk ended up reaching for a fax.Microsoft traced the outage to a problem introduced during an earlier expansion of its network capacity. The problem surfaced when the company made a subsequent network change. Microsoft ruled out a cyberattack and said AI played no role in causing the outage. Its public updates describe how servers dropped out of service, why some failed again after being restarted and how trouble in its email system reached applications well beyond Outlook. Microsoft says the Microsoft 365 outage that disrupted Outlook, Teams and Copilot for more than 24 hours is now fixed. In its final status update on the incident, the company said, “We have completed our efforts to address the underlying issue of the incident and restored service.”The disruption hit users in at least 74 countries and left businesses, governments, hospitals and airlines falling back on phone lines, paper records and, in some offices, fax machines."I want to share what we know so far. This was not a cyberattack or an issue caused by AI tooling. Our amazing team was able to work through a very challenging situation to restore service. Our investigation points to technical challenges and failure modes (cascading failures + thundering herds at our network perimeter) that made recovery more difficult than normal. I'm working closely with the engineering team to complete the full post-mortem. We will publish the post-mortem shortly covering the step-by-step timeline and our many repair items to avoid similar outages in the future. We take our responsibility to our customers seriously and will do everything we can to learn from this and prevent it going forward," wrote Charles Lamanna, EVP of Copilot, Agents, and Platform at Microsoft.The failure centred on Exchange Online, the cloud service that powers Microsoft’s business email and calendars. As servers became unavailable during routine checks, the rest had to absorb their share of requests. Microsoft said total traffic had stayed steady. Engineers found that a process used to establish secure connections was getting overwhelmed on affected machines, causing them to stop responding. With less capacity available, the usual workload was enough to put the system under pressure. [ http://www.securityweek.com] That also explains why restarting servers brought only temporary relief in some cases. A machine could appear healthy after coming back online, then stop responding as it took on work. Microsoft restricted the kinds of requests some servers received while engineers tested a configuration change on a small group of machines. The company also began reversing the recent network change. It brought traffic back in stages so engineers could see whether the servers would stay up as the workload increased.Even after people could get into their inboxes, Microsoft still had to deliver the messages that had accumulated. By Friday morning in the US, the company said the backlog had shrunk substantially, though some email could still arrive late. That made recovery hard to judge from the user’s end. Outlook could open normally while a reply approving a payment, confirming a shipment or changing a meeting time was still held up. For work that depends on a timely response, the disruption lasted until the message arrived.Exchange Online also supplies data to other Microsoft products. The calendar in Teams draws on it, as do Copilot features that retrieve work email and appointments. That meant the effects varied by task. A person could still open a file stored directly in SharePoint while a feature in the same product that needed data from Exchange could fail. The list of affected products looked long because several of them called on the same underlying service.That dependency extended to rival AI assistants. Anthropic said the outage caused errors in Claude’s Microsoft 365 integration for roughly 25 hours, disrupting requests to retrieve messages, look up appointments or search for information. OpenAI reported that users could have trouble linking Microsoft services to ChatGPT and using tools that relied on those connections. Anthropic also recorded a separate problem with signing into Claude on November 13. It specifically traced the failures in its Microsoft connector and Claude for Outlook to Microsoft’s service incident.For businesses, the outage exposed how easily a second tool can run into the same problem as the first. Opening Teams to check an appointment, or asking an AI assistant to find the email it came from, can seem like two alternatives to opening Outlook. Both still need access to data held by Exchange. The Taiwanese firm’s use of a fax was a more direct workaround. It gave the firm a way to confirm trades while its usual communications were disrupted.Microsoft has promised a full incident report. Its account so far explains how the later network change triggered the outage and why restarting machines was only part of the repair. The report still has to explain what went wrong during the original upgrade and why the subsequent change could take enough servers out of service to strain those that remained. "We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners. We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously. We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services. This was a technical issue not related to cyber or AI / agents. The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change. We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions. Given the scale of demand, we restored services gradually, validating stability at each stage. While this took longer, it helped ensure a stable restoration. We will provide a full post-incident report once our review is complete," the company said in a statement.The answer will help establish whether Microsoft can catch a similar problem while it is still confined to a small part of the network.
Article Summary: Microsoft traced the outage to a problem introduced during an earlier expansion of its network capacity. Microsoft ruled out a cyberattack and said AI played no role in causing the outage. The disruption hit users in at least 74 countries and left businesses, governments, hospitals and airlines falling back on phone lines, paper records and, in some offices, fax machines.

Article Title: Microsoft 365 outage ends after over 24 hours; Outlook, Teams restored as company says ‘underlying issue’ addressed
Article Text:
Outlook, Teams are back after more than 24 hours

Microsoft blames an earlier network upgrade for the Outlook outage

Why Outlook and Teams took almost a full day to recover

Airlines, hospitals and courts in at least 74 countries felt the Microsoft outage

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Poll Vote & Share your view What aspect of Microsoft 365's outage affected you the most? Email communications Video conferencing File sharing 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Microsoft says the Microsoft 365 outage that disrupted Outlook, Teams and Copilot for more than 24 hours is now fixed. In its final status update on the incident, the company said, “We have completed our efforts to address the underlying issue of the incident and restored service. ” The disruption hit users in at least 74 countries and left businesses, governments, hospitals and airlines falling back on phone lines, paper records and, in some offices, fax machines.The trouble began on November 12, when users in the Americas reported they could not open their Exchange Online mailboxes. Microsoft first acknowledged the issue at 5:54 pm GMT (11:24 pm IST). Just 13 minutes later, it warned that users in any region could be affected. The company has since said it is “deeply sorry” for the disruption and maintains the incident was not caused by a cyberattack or AI.According to a Microsoft spokesperson, the incident “was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change.” The company called it “a technical issue not related to cyber or AI/agents.”That explanation came after a long night of trial and error.Microsoft’s first updates on X blamed “elevated load” across several regions. Hours later, it said traffic had not gone up at all. A number of servers had become unexpectedly unavailable after failing automated health checks, and their workload landed on the servers still running, straining those too.Engineers eventually traced part of the problem to a core process on the affected servers that handles secure connections. It was getting overwhelmed, and the servers stopped processing requests. At one stage, Microsoft admitted its actions “have not provided the anticipated relief.”The hardest part was keeping servers up once they were back. Microsoft said servers it returned to service could stop responding again once they started receiving traffic. Its engineers worked on several fronts at once. They limited the types of traffic hitting affected infrastructure, rolled some servers back to an earlier configuration, patched an authentication and routing component and added virtual machines for extra capacity.Email made the job slower. Mail servers outside Microsoft keep retrying messages they could not deliver, so restored servers faced a backlog of queued mail the moment they came online. To make sure messages sent during the outage were not lost, Microsoft extended its email timeout window to 48 hours.“Given the scale of demand, we restored services gradually, validating stability at each stage. While this took longer, it helped ensure a stable restoration,” the company said.Asia Pacific was among the first regions to stabilise on November 13, followed by Europe and North America. By the afternoon of November 13 (GMT), Microsoft said email queues were “significantly reduced and approaching normal levels.” Teams chats and meetings had largely come back earlier, though calendar features that rely on Exchange Online stayed patchy for longer. Outlook.com, OneDrive, OneNote and Microsoft To Do, used on personal accounts, were hit as well.Microsoft said in January it had more than 450 million paid commercial subscriptions to its 365 services. That reach showed in who got hit.In India, the outage hit email support at IndiGo and Akasa Air. Air India rerouted its emails to keep receiving customer messages, and its flights ran as usual. At one large Indian brokerage, a backup covered for Outlook, but client calls on Teams were harder to manage.In the UK, NHS staff switched to paper records, pharmacies warned of prescription delays and a judge in Manchester sent jurors home. In Colorado, a sheriff’s office had to ask people to post bond in person, since online payments relied on Outlook email notifications. Some companies in Japan went back to fax. Even OpenAI and Anthropic ran into problems with their Microsoft 365 connectors, while electric truck maker Workhorse Group pushed its quarterly results to November 16.Investors were far calmer. Microsoft shares traded largely flat on November 13, even as the outage stretched into a second day.For users, a few loose ends may remain. Emails held in queues carry the time they were delivered rather than sent, so a message stamped November 13 may well have been written on the night of November 12.Microsoft has promised a full post-incident report once its review is complete. That report should spell out how a capacity upgrade knocked servers offline across regions for more than a day, and what the company is changing so the next network update does not do the same.
Article Summary: Microsoft blames an earlier network upgrade for the Outlook outage. The disruption hit users in at least 74 countries and left businesses, governments, hospitals and airlines falling back on phone lines, paper records and, in some offices, fax machines. Outlook, OneDrive, OneNote and Microsoft To Do, used on personal accounts, were hit as well.

Article Title: Overloaded routers and 1980s copper lines: How a network crash hit 15,000 US flights and stranded 1.5 million passengers
Article Text:
A person looks at a flight information board at LaGuardia Airport in New York, Friday, Nov. 13, 2026, after the Federal Aviation Administration grounded flights nationwide. (AP Photo/Ryan Murphy)

How overloaded routers on an old network forced a nationwide ground stop in the US

An update on 1980s-era copper lines appears to have crashed the system

The FAA's new SMART tool and a cyber-attack have both been ruled out for now

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Recovery will take days, and the question of backups is still open

For a little over four hours on November 13, not a single commercial flight was allowed to take off anywhere in the United States. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ordered a nationwide ground stop just before 4pm ET after its 22 regional air traffic control centres started losing radar data and radio contact with aircraft in patches. The order was lifted at 8:15pm ET. By then, about 15,000 flights within, into or out of the US had been delayed or cancelled, according to flight tracker FlightAware, and more than 1,600 flights on November 14 were already scrapped.The fault was not on any aircraft. It sat in the FAA's telecommunications network, which moves radar data and radio traffic between the agency's facilities. When that network started passing on unreliable data, the FAA decided controllers could not safely keep planes apart. Data firm Cirium estimates around 1.5 million people were stranded. It is only the second time since 9/11 that every departure in the country has been halted.The 22 centres hit on November 13 are Air Route Traffic Control Centers. They guide planes at cruising altitude, between takeoff and landing. They rely on a constant feed of radar returns and radio links delivered over the FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure, a network run by defence contractor L3Harris that connects more than 4,400 FAA facilities.At 3:36pm ET, switches and routers on that network became overloaded and began passing on inconsistent data. Radar coverage dropped in and out, and controllers intermittently lost contact with some aircraft. "Our switches, our routers actually got overloaded with data," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said. "They started to give us inconsistency in the data from those routers. And because of that we shut the system down. "The FAA froze departures but let the more than 3,500 planes already airborne land. Fewer than 400 were still flying by 8pm. It also extended flight plan drop times to 240 minutes at all en route centres, so filed flight plans would not time out while aircraft sat at gates. Medevac, critical cargo and law enforcement flights were exempted.Reports in the US, citing multiple sources, said an update to the network caused it to reboot, and it crashed on restart. The FAA has not confirmed this.Much of the network still runs on time-division multiplexing (TDM), an older method that sends each data stream down copper lines in fixed time slots. "We use 1980s little copper lines," Duffy said. Centres already moved to digital IP networks, which break data into packets and route them flexibly, did not fail.Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the new equipment being added to the network was "overwhelming the older system". By January 2026, the FAA had replaced 40% of its copper wiring and converted 178 radio sites, so old and new hardware now run side by side on the same network.SMART, a cloud-based planning system the FAA switched on at all 22 centres on November 10, drew suspicion. It pulls together 200 data streams, but it only sends scheduling recommendations to the FAA's command centre in Warrenton, Virginia. It does not control aircraft or carry radio traffic. Air Space Intelligence, the company behind SMART, denied any role.Mullin said investigators had found "zero evidence" of a cyber-attack, with no intrusion footprints and no claims of responsibility, though he stopped short of ruling one out.The FAA restarted traffic in tiers, releasing departures as each en route centre stabilised after engineers eased the load on the overloaded switches. Airlines now have aircraft and crews out of position, and JetBlue has already warned of cancellations continuing on November 14.The last nationwide stop, on January 11, 2023, was a different kind of failure. A database error in the NOTAM system copied itself to the backup, and departures were halted for under two hours. The November 13 failure was in the network that moves the data, and it ran more than twice as long. Why backup links did not keep the centres running has not been explained.Officials put the cost of replacing the network outright at about $50 billion. Until that happens, Duffy warned, "it's going to continue to fail."
Article Summary: Not a single commercial flight was allowed to take off anywhere in the United States for four hours on November 13. The fault was not on any aircraft. It sat in the FAA's telecommunications network, which moves radar data and radio traffic between the agency's facilities.

Article Title: Microsoft denies role in FAA ground stop that caused 10,000+ flight delays and 6,600 cancellations; company says: “We have no indication that...”
Article Text:
Microsoft: Our outage didn’t ground US flights (Image: AP)

An old FAA network, not Microsoft or AI, caused the US flight ground stop

Microsoft and FAA outages both trace back to network changes

Microsoft has denied any link between its own global outage and the air traffic control failure that grounded every departing flight in the US on Friday. More than 10,000 flights were delayed and over 6,600 cancelled, according to flight tracker FlightAware. “We have no indication that the FAA’s nationwide ground stop is related to any Microsoft services,” the company wrote on X, hours after the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) froze takeoffs nationwide.The suspicion was easy to understand. Microsoft 365 had been down since Thursday, knocking out Outlook, Teams, Copilot and even Xbox Live for users in 74 countries. Then, just before 4pm ET on Friday, the FAA’s 22 regional air traffic control centres started losing radar data and radio contact with aircraft. Two massive tech failures in two days was enough for people online to connect them. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin did not buy it. He told reporters they were “separate issues” and that he did not see “any reason to connect those two at all.”Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy put the blame on the FAA’s ageing network. “Our switches, our routers actually got overloaded with data,” he said at a White House briefing, describing a system that still runs on “1980s little copper lines.”The trouble started at 3:36pm ET, and the ground stop was lifted at 8:15pm ET. Data firm Cirium estimates around 1.5 million people were stranded.Mullin said there was “zero evidence” of a cyberattack. Asked if AI was involved, he replied, “we call it SI around here,” using the administration’s preferred term for artificial intelligence.AI was an obvious suspect. Three days earlier, the FAA had switched on SMART, an AI-powered traffic planning tool from Air Space Intelligence, at all 22 centres. The company posted on X that the ground stop “is not based on or a result of the SMART system.” Duffy was blunter. “This is not even plugged in,” he said.The two failures are unrelated, but they started in similar places. Microsoft has said it is “deeply sorry” for its outage and called it “a technical issue not related to cyber or AI / agents.” The company traced it to a flaw from an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced after a more recent network change.Think tank Anderson Economic Group estimates the lost productivity could cost close to $7 billion.At the FAA, reports citing people briefed on the matter say an update to the agency’s private telecom network, run by defence contractor L3Harris, made it reboot and then crash. Mullin’s account fits that picture. He said new equipment patched into the system “was overwhelming the older system.”Duffy now wants $50 billion in emergency funding from Congress to rebuild air traffic control, up from the $30 billion the administration had been seeking. “It’s going to continue to fail,” he warned.Microsoft is off the hook. The network that failed on Friday, built on copper lines older than Outlook itself, is the one carrying US flights again.
Article Summary: Microsoft and FAA outages both trace back to network changes. Microsoft 365 had been down since Thursday, knocking out Outlook, Teams, Copilot and even Xbox Live for users in 74 countries. The FAA’s 22 regional air traffic control centres started losing radar data and radio contact with aircraft.
